keyVerseText: Then Shephatiah the son of Mattan, and Gedaliah the son of Pashur, and Jucal the son of Shelemiah, and Pashur the son of Malchiah, heard the words that Jeremiah had spoken unto all the people, saying,
rootMeaning: The root of יוּכַל (Yûwkal) traces back to יְהוּכַל (Yᵉhûwkal), which means "Jehovah is able." This proper name embodies a declaration of God's power and sufficiency. The etymology underscores not just a personal name, but a theological affirmation that God is capable and mighty, a meaning that enriches the understanding beyond a mere label to a statement of divine ability.
usageInScripture: The word יוּכַל appears only once in Scripture, translated as "and Jucal" in Jeremiah 38:1. It is used as a proper name identifying an individual, specifically a son of Shelemiah and a servant of King Zedekiah. The consistency of its translation as a personal name reflects its role as a historical figure rather than a common noun or verb, emphasizing the importance of the name's meaning within its narrative context.
theologicalSignificance: The name יוּכַל, meaning "Jehovah is able," serves as a profound reminder of God's omnipotence within the biblical narrative. It highlights the reality that God's power undergirds the lives of His people, even in moments of crisis or uncertainty. Recognizing this name in Scripture invites believers to trust in God's ability to act on their behalf. It also points forward to the ultimate demonstration of divine power through Christ, who embodies God's ability to save and sustain. Thus, this name enriches faith by anchoring it in the assurance of God's unwavering capability.
keyVerseReflection: In Jeremiah 38:1, Jucal is listed alongside other officials who heard Jeremiah's words to the people. The mention of Jucal, whose name means "Jehovah is able," subtly reinforces the presence of God's power amid the political and spiritual turmoil of the time. His role as a servant of King Zedekiah who interacts with the prophet Jeremiah highlights the tension between human authority and divine sovereignty, with the name reminding readers that ultimately, it is God who is able to deliver and guide His people.
